title: Treatment for acute anterior cruciate ligament tear: five year outcome of randomised trial
question: In young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction give better knee outcomes at five years than rehabilitation with the option of a later reconstruction?

bottom_line.question: In young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction give better knee outcomes at five years than rehabilitation with the option of a later reconstruction?
bottom_line.answer: Early reconstruction was no better at five years: the KOOS4 knee score improved by 42.9 points with early reconstruction and 44.9 points with rehabilitation plus optional later reconstruction (difference 2.0 points, P=0.54), so rehabilitation can be offered as the first treatment.

sections.title: The Question: Surgery First or Rehabilitation First?
sections.markdown:
Early surgery for a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), one of the main ligaments that stabilises the knee, did no better over five years than trying rehabilitation first. That is the result of the KANON trial in Sweden. An ACL tear is a common and serious injury in young, active people. It can leave a knee that feels unreliable, lower activity levels and worse quality of life. Many patients go on to develop knee osteoarthritis whatever treatment they receive.

One standard response is **ACL reconstruction**, surgery that replaces the torn ligament with a graft taken from one of the patient's own tendons. The alternative is structured rehabilitation (supervised exercise therapy), with surgery only if the knee keeps giving way. Doctors have long debated how much each approach contributes to short-term and long-term results.

KANON compared these two strategies directly. At two years it found no difference in patient reported outcomes. This report follows the same patients to five years and adds X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis and a count of meniscus operations. The authors describe it as the first mid-term randomised comparison of the two strategies.

sections.title: How the Trial Was Designed and Measured
sections.markdown:
## How the trial worked

The researchers enrolled 121 active adults aged 18 to 35 (average age 26) at two Swedish hospitals. Each had an ACL tear no more than four weeks old in a knee that had never been injured before. The trial excluded professional athletes, people who were less than moderately active, and patients with some other serious knee damage.

Everyone received the same structured rehabilitation. In addition, patients were randomly assigned to one of two strategies:

- Early reconstruction (62 patients), done within 10 weeks of injury by one of four experienced knee surgeons.
- Optional delayed reconstruction (59 patients). These patients had surgery only if the knee became unstable enough to cause symptoms and a positive pivot shift test confirmed it. In that exam, the doctor feels the shinbone slip out of place.

Each surgeon chose whether to take the graft from the patellar tendon (below the kneecap) or from the hamstrings. In both groups, torn menisci (the cartilage pads that cushion the knee) were trimmed or repaired when needed. Only one patient was lost by five years, which left 120 for analysis.

## What was measured

The main measure was the **KOOS** (Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score), a questionnaire that patients fill in themselves. It has five subscales: pain, symptoms, daily function, sport and recreation function, and knee-related quality of life. Each is scored from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). KOOS4 is the average of four of these subscales, and the primary outcome was how much it improved:

main outcome = KOOS4 at five years minus KOOS4 at the start of the trial

The researchers sized the trial so that 120 patients gave an 80% chance of detecting a 10-point difference between the groups.

The other outcomes were:

- general health (the SF-36 survey)
- activity level (the Tegner scale, 1 to 10) and whether patients returned to their pre-injury activity level
- knee stability on two hands-on tests (Lachman and pivot shift)
- meniscus surgery
- osteoarthritis on weight-bearing X-rays

A radiologist who did not know which group each patient was in graded the X-rays. The radiologist looked for bony spurs and narrowing of the joint space, the standard signs of osteoarthritis.

The results were analysed in two ways. The **full analysis set** compares patients by the group they were randomly assigned to, whatever surgery they had later. This tests the strategy. The as treated analysis compares patients by what they actually received: early surgery, delayed surgery or rehabilitation alone. This tests the treatments.

sections.title: How Patients Fared: Surgery Rates, Symptoms and Knee Stability
sections.markdown:
## Half the rehabilitation group never had surgery

Of the 59 patients offered delayed reconstruction, 30 (51%) had it within five years, seven of them between years two and five. The other 29 managed with rehabilitation alone. Across the whole trial, 61 patients had early reconstruction, 30 had delayed reconstruction and 29 had none.

## No difference in how patients felt

Both groups improved a great deal. KOOS4 rose by an average of 42.9 points with early reconstruction and 44.9 points with optional delayed reconstruction. The paper reports a difference between the groups of 2.0 points (95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjusting for starting scores). The whole interval stays within the 10-point difference the trial was designed to detect.

At five years there were no significant differences in:

- KOOS4 itself (P=0.45)
- any KOOS subscale
- SF-36 physical or mental scores
- Tegner activity level
- return to pre-injury activity

The as treated analysis gave the same picture: early surgery, late surgery and no surgery ended up in similar places. Return to pre-injury activity was modest overall. This matches a meta-analysis of 5,770 reconstruction patients, in which only 63% got back to their previous activity level and 44% returned to competitive sport.

## Tighter knees, same outcomes

Surgery did make knees more stable. At five years, knees in the early reconstruction group were significantly more likely to pass the Lachman and pivot shift tests (both P<0.001). That mechanical difference did not show up in pain, function, activity or quality of life.

sections.title: Osteoarthritis, Meniscus Surgery and Graft Failures
sections.markdown:
## Osteoarthritis appeared early, whatever the treatment

X-rays were available for 113 knees, and none showed osteoarthritis at the start. By five years:

- 12% had osteoarthritis in the main joint between the thighbone and shinbone (tibiofemoral).
- 19% had it behind the kneecap (patellofemoral).

The randomised groups did not differ significantly (P=0.17).

Comparing by treatment received:

- Reconstructed knees: 11% tibiofemoral and 23% patellofemoral osteoarthritis.
- Knees treated with rehabilitation alone: 12% and 8%.

Neither gap was statistically significant (P=0.995 and P=0.084). Among reconstructed knees, patellar tendon grafts were linked to significantly more osteoarthritis behind the kneecap than hamstring grafts (P=0.001). The authors point to evidence that the patellar tendon can shorten after surgery, changing how load passes through the joint behind the kneecap.

The authors call it striking that this much osteoarthritis appears five years after an injury at around age 30. They conclude that reconstruction does not protect the knee from these structural changes. Earlier long-term studies, including a 15-year randomised trial, also found no difference in osteoarthritis between treatments.

## Meniscus surgery and graft failures

Observational studies have suggested that waiting longer before reconstruction leads to more meniscus injury. The authors note that those studies suffer from confounding: patients who get early surgery and patients who get late surgery differ in ways that affect the outcome.

In this trial, 61 of 120 knees (51%) had meniscus surgery over five years: 29 in the early group and 32 in the delayed-option group (P=0.48). A time-to-event analysis, which accounts for when each meniscus was operated on, also found no difference (P=0.77). The early group did have fewer meniscus operations in total once repeat operations on the same meniscus were counted. That result is exploratory and appears in the supplementary appendix.

Four grafts ruptured: three of the 61 early reconstructions (5%) and one of the 30 delayed ones (3%). That is in line with the 4.3% rate found in a five-year follow-up of 1,415 reconstruction patients.

sections.title: What It Means for Patients and Doctors
sections.markdown:
## What it means

In young, active adults with a fresh ACL tear, early reconstruction plus rehabilitation did no better than rehabilitation first with surgery held in reserve. This held for patient reported outcomes, osteoarthritis and meniscus surgery. Under the second strategy, about half the patients never needed a reconstruction, and the trial found no evidence that either approach did more harm. The authors conclude that clinicians and patients should consider rehabilitation as a primary treatment option.

The results do not apply to professional athletes or to people who are less than moderately active, because neither group was enrolled. Patients and doctors learned the group assignments after two years. However, the five-year X-ray analysis was planned in the original protocol, and the radiologist grading the images did not know each patient's treatment.

sources.abstract: Objective To compare, in young active adults with an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, the mid-term (five year) patient reported and radiographic outcomes between those treated with rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and those treated with rehabilitation and optional delayed ACL reconstruction. Design Extended follow-up of prospective randomised controlled trial. Setting Orthopaedic departments at two hospitals in Sweden. Participants 121 young, active adults (mean age 26 years) with acute ACL injury to a previously uninjured knee. One patient was lost to five year follow-up. Intervention All patients received similar structured rehabilitation. In addition to rehabilitation, 62 patients were assigned to early ACL reconstruction and 59 were assigned to the option of having a delayed ACL reconstruction if needed. Main outcome measure The main outcome was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five subscales of the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS4). Other outcomes included the absolute KOOS4 score, all five KOOS subscale scores, SF-36, Tegner activity scale, meniscal surgery, and radiographic osteoarthritis at five years. Results Thirty (51%) patients assigned to optional delayed ACL reconstruction had delayed ACL reconstruction (seven between two and five years). The mean change in KOOS4 score from baseline to five years was 42.9 points for those assigned to rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and 44.9 for those assigned to rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction (between group difference 2.0 points, 95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjustment for baseline score). At five years, no significant between group differences were seen in KOOS4 (P=0.45), any of the KOOS subscales (P≥0.12), SF-36 (P≥0.34), Tegner activity scale (P=0.74), or incident radiographic osteoarthritis of the index knee (P=0.17). sources.sec-characteristics-of-patients-and-trea: Thirty (51%) patients assigned to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction chose to have (and had) a delayed anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction over the five year period (seven in the period between two and five years; median 867 (range 743-1695) days after injury) (fig 1). Fifteen anterior cruciate ligaments were reconstructed using patella tendon procedures and 15 using hamstrings tendon procedures. Over the five year period, 61 patients had an early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, 30 had a delayed reconstruction, and 29 were treated with rehabilitation alone. Of the 91 primary reconstructions performed, 40 used patella tendon procedures and 51 used hamstrings tendon procedures.

Despite several contacts by mail and telephone, one patient assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction did not attend the five year clinical visit. Consequently, we included 120/121 participants in this five year follow-up report, 61 of whom were assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and 59 to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction if needed (table 1). Two patients assigned to early reconstruction did not have reconstruction or had less than 10 rehabilitation visits; we excluded them from the as treated analysis but included them in the full analysis set.
sources.sec-patient-reported-outcomes-5/p1: Patient reported outcomes included the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS), the Medical Outcomes Study 36-item short-form health survey (SF-36), and the Tegner activity scale. Consistent with our previous publication, the main outcome of this report was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five KOOS subscales (KOOS4). Other outcomes include the crude KOOS4 score, all five separate KOOS subscales, the scores on the SF-36 physical and mental components (all 0-100 scales, worst to best), and the Tegner activity scale score (1-10, lowest to highest) at five years. In addition, we report return to pre-injury activity level as patients who reported similar or higher Tegner activity scale scores at five years compared with their pre-injury scores.
sources.sec-participants-3/p1: We enrolled active adults, 18 to 35 years of age, with an anterior cruciate ligament tear not more than four weeks old to a previously uninjured knee at the departments of orthopaedics at Skåne University Hospital and Helsingborg Hospital, Sweden (table 1). Major exclusion criteria were professional athletes (10 on the Tegner activity score; 0-10, lowest to highest activity level), less than moderately active people (<5 on the same scale), a total collateral ligament rupture, a full thickness cartilage lesion visualised on magnetic resonance imaging, and extensive meniscal fixation. Details of the recruitment process, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the randomisation process have been published. All patients provided fully informed written consent to participate in the study.
